title: The hypertrophy series: picking your progression battles to push tonnage
summary: Past the novice phase you cannot progress on everything at once, but specializing on one lift while neglecting others leads to yo-yo training. NH argues for using volume/intensity manipulation inside a flexible body part split to push some patterns while deliberately holding others stable, so total tonnage keeps rising without regression.

claims.claim: Past the novice phase you cannot progress on every lift at the same rate.
Focusing solely on one pattern (e.g. only deadlifting for a month) makes that lift improve faster but is counterproductive for overall tonnage and hypertrophy because the rest is neglected.
Rotating single-lift focus phases causes yo-yo training: when you return to the first lift you have regressed, sometimes back to baseline.
The goal is steady progression plus stability, so strength and therefore tonnage never go down.
Pick your battles: use volume and intensity manipulation to promote certain lifts and de-emphasize others, within a flexible program, without switching programs.
Build programs from the ground up, starting minimalist and adding one lift or variable at a time, so you know what every element does and can manipulate a complex program confidently.
In a cyclical body part split where lifts aren't rotated out monthly, de-emphasized lifts still get enough frequency that they never regress.
This is the best way to bring up weak points, because it avoids suddenly shocking a body part with a big jump in volume, which is always bad.
If you push tonnage up in one area, something else must come down, because muscles and structures such as the lower back are shared between lifts.
Trying to progress squat and deadlift simultaneously overloads the shared lower back and invites injury and regression.
Example: to prioritize the deadlift (glutes, hamstrings, lower back), cut knee-flexion tonnage by switching to high-intensity, low-volume squatting with the same weight to maintain strength.
Being stagnant on a lift is not stalling if you deliberately chose it; once hinges are where you want, switch priority to squats.
Alternating priority in this way produces a staircase (up, stagnant, up, stagnant) so overall tonnage keeps climbing and never drops.
